title: TCP U2·W3 — Personal Financial Planning (2026)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the whole financial picture

Tax planning sits inside a broader personal financial plan — retirement, education, insurance, Social Security, and charitable giving — where tax efficiency and life goals meet. A CPA advising a business owner like Jordan Reed integrates these so that the after-tax outcome serves the family's objectives. This week surveys the major personal financial planning areas and their tax dimensions, on the 2026 baseline, completing the individual-side planning the discipline tests.

Retirement plan choices

Retirement accounts are the foundation. Traditional IRAs and 401(k)s deduct contributions now and tax withdrawals later; Roth versions forgo the deduction for tax-free qualified withdrawals — a bet that pays off when future rates are higher. For business owners, SEP-IRAs, SIMPLE plans, solo 401(k)s, and defined-benefit plans allow far larger deductible contributions. Key rules a planner manages: annual contribution limits, the 10% early-withdrawal penalty before 59½, and required minimum distributions (RMDs) beginning at the statutory age (Roth IRAs have no lifetime RMDs). Choosing and funding the right plan is often the largest single tax deduction an owner can take.

Roth strategy

The Roth decision is a recurring planning lever. Beyond direct contributions (limited by income), a backdoor Roth (nondeductible IRA then conversion) reaches high earners, and a Roth conversion in a low-income year — a year with a business loss or before RMDs and Social Security begin — fills up low brackets cheaply and moves future growth to tax-free status. Roth accounts also help heirs (no income tax on inherited Roth withdrawals) and avoid the RMD drawdown. The planner times conversions across years to manage the marginal rate, the same bracket-management logic from the income side.

Education funding

Funding education tax-efficiently uses dedicated vehicles. 529 plans grow tax-free for qualified education expenses, accept large contributions (with five-year gift-tax superfunding), and are now usable for some K-12 and apprenticeship costs; Coverdell ESAs are a smaller alternative with more investment flexibility. These coordinate with the education credits (AOTC/Lifetime Learning) from Unit 1 — the same expense cannot be used for both a tax-free 529 distribution and a credit, so the planner allocates expenses to maximize the combined benefit. Education funding is also a gifting strategy, moving wealth to the next generation within the annual exclusion.

Insurance in the plan

Insurance manages risk and carries tax features. Life insurance pays a tax-free death benefit and, in permanent forms, accumulates cash value tax-deferred; it provides estate liquidity to pay taxes and equalize inheritances, and an irrevocable life insurance trust (ILIT) keeps the proceeds out of the taxable estate. Disability insurance replaces income (benefits are tax-free if the individual paid the premiums with after-tax dollars), and long-term-care coverage protects assets against care costs. The planner sizes coverage to the family's needs and structures ownership to optimize the tax and estate result.

Social Security planning

Social Security claiming is a consequential timing decision. Benefits can start at 62 (permanently reduced), at full retirement age, or be delayed to 70 (increased by delayed-retirement credits) — delaying is effectively a guaranteed, inflation-adjusted return that benefits those with longevity and other income to bridge the gap. Benefits are partially taxable (up to 85%) depending on "combined income," so coordinating Social Security with IRA withdrawals and Roth conversions manages that taxation. Spousal and survivor strategies add further optimization for married couples.

Charitable planning vehicles

Charitable giving combines philanthropy with tax efficiency through specialized vehicles. A donor-advised fund (DAF) gives an immediate deduction while distributing to charities over time (ideal for bunching). A charitable remainder trust (CRT) pays the donor an income stream with the remainder to charity — useful to diversify a low-basis asset without immediate capital-gains tax. A charitable lead trust (CLT) reverses the flow. A qualified charitable distribution (QCD) from an IRA (after the eligible age) sends up to a limit directly to charity, satisfying the RMD and excluding it from income entirely — often better than a deduction. The vehicle is chosen to match the asset, the timing, and the donor's income needs.

Integration — the financial plan as one system

The discipline's lesson is integration: retirement, education, insurance, Social Security, and charitable decisions interact with the income tax, the transfer tax, and the entity plan. A Roth conversion affects Social Security taxation and Medicare premiums; a CRT funds retirement income and a charitable legacy at once; life insurance provides the liquidity to pay the estate tax that the wealth-transfer plan defers. The planner optimizes the whole system across the client's lifetime and beyond — the comprehensive judgment that the CPA's planning role, and the TCP discipline, are built to deliver.

Asset location and the tax-efficient portfolio

How investments are placed across account types — asset location — is a quiet but powerful lever. Tax-inefficient assets (taxable bonds, REITs, actively traded funds throwing off ordinary income) belong in tax-deferred or Roth accounts, while tax-efficient assets (index funds, municipal bonds, buy-and-hold stock taxed at preferential long-term rates) belong in taxable accounts. Within taxable accounts, tax-loss harvesting and holding for long-term rates improve after-tax return. Coordinating asset location with asset allocation (the risk mix) lets a planner raise the family's after-tax return without changing the investment risk — a benefit that compounds over decades.

Estate liquidity and the integrated plan

A wealth-transfer plan can defer tax yet leave the estate illiquid — rich in business interests and real estate but short of cash to pay an estate-tax bill or equalize inheritances among heirs. Life insurance (often in an ILIT) supplies that liquidity; installment payment of estate tax under §6166 helps when a closely held business dominates the estate; and buy-sell agreements funded with insurance ensure a smooth ownership transition. The financial planner stress-tests the estate for liquidity as deliberately as for tax — because a plan that minimizes tax but forces a fire sale of the business has failed the family it was meant to serve.

CMA bridge

For Jordan Reed, personal financial planning is the other half of business success: funding a defined-benefit plan through MBG for a large deduction, timing Roth conversions in lean construction years, using life insurance in an ILIT for estate liquidity, and giving appreciated business interests through a CRT. The CFO who plans the owner's finances alongside the company's captures value across both balance sheets.

Practice and recap

  1. Choose retirement plans (traditional vs Roth; SEP/SIMPLE/solo 401(k)/DB for owners); manage contribution limits, the 10% early-withdrawal penalty, and RMDs.
  2. Time Roth conversions into low-income years; use backdoor Roth for high earners.
  3. Fund education with 529 (superfunding) / Coverdell, coordinated with education credits; structure insurance (tax-free death benefit, ILIT, disability) for risk and estate liquidity.
  4. Plan Social Security claiming (62 vs FRA vs 70; up to 85% taxable) and charitable vehicles (DAF, CRT/CLT, QCD) to match asset, timing, and income needs.

Recap: personal financial planning integrates retirement (traditional vs Roth, owner plans, RMDs and the early-withdrawal penalty), Roth-conversion timing into low-income years, education funding (529 superfunding, coordinated with credits), insurance (tax-free death benefit, ILIT for estate liquidity, disability), Social Security claiming (62/FRA/70, up to 85% taxable), and charitable vehicles (DAF, CRT/CLT, QCD) — all optimized as one system across the income tax, transfer tax, and entity plan over the client's lifetime.

flashcards.back: Traditional: deduct now, tax withdrawals later. Roth: no deduction, tax-free qualified withdrawals (bet on higher future rates), no lifetime RMDs, better for heirs.
SEP-IRA, SIMPLE, solo 401(k), defined-benefit plans allow large deductible contributions — often an owner's biggest single deduction. Watch 10% early-withdrawal penalty (<59½) and RMDs.
Convert in a low-income year (business loss; before RMDs/Social Security) to fill low brackets cheaply; backdoor Roth (nondeductible IRA → conversion) for high earners.
529: tax-free for qualified education, superfunding (5 yrs of exclusions). Coverdell: smaller, flexible. Can't use the same expense for a tax-free 529 distribution AND an education credit.
Tax-free death benefit; permanent policies grow cash value tax-deferred; provides estate liquidity; an ILIT keeps proceeds out of the taxable estate.
62 (reduced) / full retirement age / delay to 70 (increased). Up to 85% of benefits taxable based on combined income — coordinate with IRA withdrawals/Roth conversions.
Pays the donor income, remainder to charity; lets a donor diversify a low-basis asset without immediate capital-gains tax + a partial deduction.
Direct IRA-to-charity transfer (after eligible age) up to a limit; satisfies the RMD and is excluded from income — often better than a deduction.

questions.q: A Roth IRA differs from a traditional IRA in that qualified withdrawals are:
questions.explain: Roth contributions are not deductible, but qualified withdrawals are tax-free; Roth IRAs also have no lifetime RMDs.

questions.q: The best time to execute a Roth conversion is generally a year with:
questions.explain: Converting in a low-bracket year fills low brackets cheaply and moves growth to tax-free status.

questions.q: A 10% penalty generally applies to IRA withdrawals taken before age:
questions.explain: The 10% early-withdrawal penalty applies before age 59½ (with exceptions).

questions.q: A qualified charitable distribution (QCD) from an IRA:
choices: Satisfies the RMD and is excluded from income
questions.explain: A QCD goes directly to charity, counts toward the RMD, and is excluded from income.

questions.q: Delaying Social Security from full retirement age to 70:
choices: Increases the monthly benefit via delayed-retirement credits
questions.explain: Delaying past full retirement age earns delayed-retirement credits, raising the benefit.

questions.q: A charitable remainder trust (CRT) lets a donor:
choices: Diversify a low-basis asset without immediate capital-gains tax, keeping an income stream
questions.explain: A CRT pays the donor income with the remainder to charity, deferring gain on a contributed low-basis asset.

questions.q: Life insurance held in an irrevocable life insurance trust (ILIT) primarily:
choices: Keeps the death proceeds out of the taxable estate
questions.explain: An ILIT removes the policy proceeds from the insured's taxable estate while providing liquidity.
